title: JuryProbe: An Empirical Consensus-Risk Diagnostic for Routing Reference-Free Factuality Judge Panels to Grounded Verification
summary: JuryProbe tests whether agreement among reference-free factuality judges hides shared errors, then uses calibration evidence to decide when accepted claims need grounded verification.
contributions: A labeled calibration probe measures correlated missed corruptions and excess unanimous false acceptance. When panel-level risk is flagged, every reference-free majority acceptance is rechecked by the same judges with references.
On Number and Entity corruptions, false-negative correlations over all corrupted claims were 0.402 and 0.368. False-consensus lifts on GPT-4o-detectable subsets were 3.13× and 18.13×, respectively.

All 34 flagged splits matched the Ground-All-Accepts policy. On a constructed negative control, stand-down avoided reference acquisition for about 28% of deployment claims, with a 0.004 absolute false-accept-rate increase versus Ground-All-Accepts.
limitations: The diagnostic offers no formal risk guarantee and does not establish reliable stand-down for natural panels.
Trusted-reference experiments are best-case diagnostics. Weak retrieval reduces true-accept coverage, and distribution shifts require recalibration.

abstract.text: Panels of inexpensive LLM judges increasingly make accept-or-escalate decisions. In factuality settings, accepting a claim because several reference-free judges agree can create a hidden risk: agreement may reflect shared false-negative blind spots rather than independent evidence. We introduce JuryProbe, an empirical consensus-risk diagnostic for reference-free factuality judge panels, paired with a calibration-based routing policy. JuryProbe estimates consensus risk from a labeled calibration probe using false-negative-only (FN-only) judge correlation and false-consensus lift; when flagged high-risk, reference-free majority accepts are routed to the same judges with trusted references. On audited FEVER corruptions, reference-free panels show correlated false negatives (FN-only correlations 0.402 and 0.368; lifts 3.13x and 18.13x), while unanimous false consensus drops to zero under a trusted-reference best-case diagnostic on both minimal-pair and non-minimal-pair evidence. In flagged settings, the routed policy is by construction equivalent to grounding every reference-free majority accept (verified in 34/34 splits): improvement comes from accept-conditioned grounding, while the diagnostic determines whether to activate it. A fixed, pre-specified rule flags 8-10 of 10 splits across synthetic, benchmark-authored, and scientific families and 0 of 10 on a negative control, where standing down avoids 28% of reference acquisitions at a 0.004 increase in false accepts. False-accept reduction persists under weak BM25 retrieval at substantial coverage cost, while stale stand-down labels require periodic recalibration. JuryProbe provides no formal risk guarantee and does not establish reliable stand-down on natural panels; its supported contribution is an empirical diagnostic of high-risk panel error dependence.

researcher_questions.question: Are multiple agreeing LLM judges reliable evidence of factual correctness?
researcher_questions.answer: Not automatically. Different reference-free judges can miss the same factual corruption, so unanimous agreement can be wrong. JuryProbe measures shared false-negative errors on labeled calibration claims using false-negative correlation and false-consensus lift. It assesses a panel’s risk regime, rather than certifying each new claim.

researcher_questions.question: What is false unanimous consensus, and how does JuryProbe measure it?
researcher_questions.answer: False unanimous consensus occurs when every judge accepts a corrupted claim. False-consensus lift compares the observed unanimous false-accept rate with the rate expected if the judges’ errors were independent. A lift above one indicates excess joint failure on that evaluation subset. Table 1 reports false-negative correlations over all corrupted claims separately from lift on the GPT-4o-detectable subset; these quantities have different sample scopes.

researcher_questions.question: How does JuryProbe differ from disagreement-based escalation?
researcher_questions.answer: Disagreement routing cannot catch a corrupted claim accepted unanimously. When calibration flags a panel, JuryProbe rechecks every majority acceptance with references, including unanimous accepts. An unflagged panel is not certified safe.

researcher_questions.question: Does evidence grounding eliminate correlated errors in LLM judges?
researcher_questions.answer: No. No unanimous false consensus was observed with trusted references in the tested Number/Entity FEVER subsets and SciFact diagnostic, but this does not establish error independence or a universal guarantee. On SciFact, pairwise false-negative correlation remained positive with rationale or full-abstract evidence, even though no unanimous false consensus was observed. Grounding and independent errors are different claims.

researcher_questions.question: What changes when references come from weak retrieval?
researcher_questions.answer: Evidence quality matters. In the BM25 retrieval stress test, grounding reduced false accepts but also reduced acceptance of clean claims. This is a coverage tradeoff, not evidence that weak retrieval outperforms trusted references. Trusted-reference results are best-case diagnostics, rather than a guarantee for a deployed retrieval system.

researcher_questions.question: Can an unflagged judge panel safely skip verification?
researcher_questions.answer: JuryProbe provides no formal risk guarantee and does not establish reliable stand-down for natural panels. Its routing decision comes from a labeled calibration probe, not a per-claim safety score. When judges or the claim distribution change, stale calibration can miss renewed consensus risk; the paper studies periodic recalibration as a response.

citation_context: Relevant when discussing shared false-negative errors in reference-free factuality judge panels, panel-level calibration diagnostics, or accept-conditioned grounded verification. It does not establish that an unflagged panel is safe.

title: ModularSQL: A Runtime Guardrail for the Multiplicity Blind Spot in Text-to-SQL
summary: ModularSQL checks executed SQL results for multiplicity problems that set-collapsing evaluation can miss. It combines a duplicate-preserving metric with selective runtime intervention.
contributions: Multiset-EX retains duplicate counts while ignoring row order. A post-selection detector triggers deterministic DISTINCT patches or candidate-based LLM rescue.
Across three released DeepEye-SQL backbones, Set-EX exceeded Multiset-EX by 5.81–6.79 percentage points on 1,532 executable BIRD-Dev queries.

The Qwen3-Coder reproduction improved Multiset-EX from 65.86% to 67.75%, preserving 72.06% Set-EX. In the reported 1,532-query run, it flagged 77 anomalies, with $0.0076 total additional LLM cost and 120 ms amortized overhead per query.
limitations: Experiments cover BIRD-Dev with SQLite. Full candidate-based rescue was tested only with the DeepEye-SQL reproduction; candidate-free components transferred to two other released prediction sets.
Deterministic patches address DISTINCT changes, not general aggregation or join repair. No additional full repair-round comparison was performed.

abstract.text: Text-to-SQL systems are increasingly deployed on production databases, where queries that pass benchmark evaluation can still produce results that distort downstream workflows. Standard set-based execution accuracy (Set-EX) collapses duplicate rows and can therefore miss multiplicity errors, including missing DISTINCT, inflated aggregates, and Cartesian-style join explosions. We call this the Multiplicity Blind Spot (MBS) and introduce Multiset-EX, a multiplicity-preserving evaluation criterion that exposes such failures. Across released DeepEye-SQL artifacts from three backbones (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, and Gemma-3-27B) on executable BIRD-Dev N=1532, we find a consistent 5.81--6.79 pp gap between Set-EX and Multiset-EX. The gap is not specific to DeepEye-SQL: it persists on released DAIL-SQL+GPT-4 (5.22 pp) and BIRD GPT-3.5-turbo (3.39 pp) predictions. We further introduce ModularSQL, a lightweight post-selection runtime guardrail that probes executed results for multiplicity anomalies and applies deterministic patches or low-cost LLM rescue only to flagged queries. Integrated with DeepEye-SQL using Qwen3-Coder, ModularSQL preserves Set-EX at 72.06% while improving Multiset-EX from 65.86% to 67.75% (+1.89 pp). It flags 77 high-risk anomalies, while adding only $0.0076 in total LLM cost and 120 ms amortized latency per query. Cross-pipeline evaluation shows that the candidate-free detector and deterministic patches also transfer to independently released prediction sets. Overall, these results show that benchmark accuracy does not necessarily imply execution-safe SQL, and that lightweight, multiplicity-aware runtime guardrails can narrow this gap with modest computational overhead.

researcher_questions.question: What can set-based SQL evaluation miss?
researcher_questions.answer: Two query outputs can contain the same distinct rows but different duplicate counts. BIRD’s set-collapsing comparison can hide that difference; Multiset-EX preserves it. This limitation does not apply to every Text-to-SQL evaluator: Spider’s test-suite evaluator already compares multisets.

researcher_questions.question: What does ModularSQL need at runtime?
researcher_questions.answer: The detector uses the selected SQL and its database result. Full LLM rescue also needs upstream candidates; without them, only the detector and deterministic patches apply. An anomaly is a review signal, not proof of an error. Normal-looking semantic errors can pass undetected.

citation_context: Relevant when discussing duplicate-sensitive Text-to-SQL evaluation, the limits of set-collapsing execution accuracy, or selective post-selection runtime intervention. The reported experiments use BIRD-Dev and SQLite.

title: When Does Dynamic Ensembling Pay Off? Diagnosing Regionwise Gains in Regression under Distribution Shift
summary: This study asks when a small labeled target-domain probe can identify useful regional reweighting of a frozen regression-model pool under distribution shift.
contributions: D_CF5 cross-fits the risk difference between regional and global convex blends. A separate Probe-Validated Ensemble Selector compares candidates against a static-convex floor using held-out validation; the selector does not use D_CF5 as an input.
The diagnostic correlated with realized regional gains at Spearman +0.98 across 12 dataset-shift pairs and +0.83 in a 16-pair sensitivity analysis.
The prospective selector matched or improved its static floor in all 12 runs. Two Seoul Bike deployments reduced test risk by 11% and 16%; the other ten runs retained the static floor.
limitations: The diagnostic targets regional convex reweighting, not every dynamic adaptation mechanism. It requires labeled target observations.
The gate uses asymptotic validation, not a finite-sample guarantee. Evidence primarily concerns tabular regression with frozen source models and within-project preregistration.

abstract.text: Whether input-dependent ("dynamic") combination of a regression model pool beats the best static blend depends on the shift and is rarely known before deployment. Can a small labeled target-domain probe tell us when reallocating trust across regions of the input space will pay off? We answer this with D̂_CF5, which estimates from the probe the cross-fitted gain of the regionwise convex combination over the best static convex blend: the realizable value of deciding, region by region, whom to trust. Across a frozen suite of 12 dataset-shift pairs (spatial, temporal, domain, feature-cluster), D̂_CF5 predicts realized regionwise test gains with dataset-level Spearman +0.98 (95% CI [+0.83, +1.00]; p = 5 × 10⁻⁵), including two cases overturning preregistered expectations. The relationship holds in a 16-pair sensitivity analysis (Spearman +0.83), whereas alternative probe diagnostics reach at most +0.66. This contrast isolates regional trust reallocation: correlation is +0.98 for regionwise-convex gain, but +0.01 for smooth covariate-dependent stacking after affine correction. A controlled generator shows dynamic gains arise from the interaction of shift heterogeneity and local competence, increase with shift severity, and become realizable between 128 and 256 probe labels in the tested grid. The Probe-Validated Ensemble Selector chooses among a static affine stacker and dynamic realizers, deploying a candidate only when a held-out lower confidence bound clears the static-convex floor. In a preregistered prospective batch, it matched or improved the floor in all 12 runs; two deployments reduced test risk by 11% and 16%, while the gate rejected a candidate whose un-gated deployment incurred >30× the static loss. We release OpenRegShift, a reproducible evaluation harness for regression ensembles under distribution shift.

researcher_questions.question: How many target labels does this protocol use?
researcher_questions.answer: The main protocol uses 512 labeled target observations: 205 for diagnosis, 215 for fitting candidate combinations and 92 for validation. Base regressors stay frozen. Target test data are reserved for final evaluation, so this is not an unlabeled adaptation method.

researcher_questions.question: Does a low diagnostic value rule out all dynamic ensembles?
researcher_questions.answer: No. D_CF5 targets regional convex reweighting. In two Seoul Bike runs, a separate held-out selector accepted smooth covariate-dependent stacking despite a near-zero regional diagnostic. The selector does not take D_CF5 as input.

citation_context: Relevant when discussing probe-based diagnosis of regional convex ensemble gains under distribution shift, or held-out validation of frozen-model combinations. The diagnostic is not a universal predictor of dynamic-ensemble gains.
